articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Backlog Heads Into Hurricane Season
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, drainage projects remain stalled in Brownsville, Myrtle Grove, and Brent. County engineers say they're still catching up from decades of deferred maintenance.
brief: Escambia County has completed only 12 of 67 priority stormwater projects since voters approved a dedicated drainage fee in 2023
Engineers estimate $47 million in unfunded repairs across flood-prone neighborhoods including Brownsville, Myrtle Grove, and Brent
County officials cite supply chain delays and staffing shortages while residents prepare for another hurricane season with failing infrastructure
articles.body:
The ditch behind Clarence Williams' house on Pace Boulevard hasn't drained properly since 2019. Every heavy rain sends water pooling against his foundation, creeping toward the back door of the Brownsville home where he's lived for 34 years.

"They came out here, took pictures, said we were on the list," Williams said last week, standing in his backyard where the grass stays permanently soggy. "That was two years ago. Nothing."

Williams' drainage problem sits somewhere in a queue of 55 unfinished stormwater projects across Escambia County. Together they represent $47 million in deferred maintenance heading into the 2026 hurricane season with no clear timeline for completion.

Three years after county voters approved a dedicated stormwater fee—$4.50 per month for residential properties—the infrastructure backlog has barely budged. The fee generates roughly $8.2 million annually. At that rate, the county would need nearly six years of dedicated funding just to address current priorities. New problems keep getting added to the list.

Decades of Deferred Work

The stormwater fee passed in November 2023 with 58% approval after county officials warned of failing drainage systems throughout unincorporated areas. Campaign materials promised "systematic investment" in neighborhoods that had been flooding for decades.

Escambia County Public Works Director Maria Gonzalez said the fee has funded progress. But she acknowledged the scale of the problem exceeds available resources.

"We're dealing with infrastructure that should have been maintained starting in the 1970s," Gonzalez told county commissioners at a June budget workshop. "Some of these systems were never built to modern standards. Some were never completed at all."

County records show 12 stormwater projects completed since the fee took effect in January 2024. Most were smaller repairs—pipe replacements, inlet upgrades, ditch clearing. The larger capital projects in Brownsville, Myrtle Grove, and Brent remain in design phases or waiting for permits.

A $3.8 million drainage overhaul for the Brent Lane corridor has been in engineering review for 18 months. The Myrtle Grove retention pond expansion, budgeted at $2.1 million, awaits environmental permits from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Brownsville's comprehensive drainage study, completed in 2024, identified $12 million in needed repairs. None have been funded.

Supply Chain and Staffing

Gonzalez pointed to factors beyond the county's control. Concrete pipe manufacturers are quoting 16-week lead times. Specialized equipment for drainage work requires booking months in advance. The county's engineering department has three vacant positions it cannot fill at current salary levels.

"We're competing with private developers for the same contractors, the same materials," Gonzalez said. "And they can pay more."

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose District 1 includes Brownsville, expressed frustration at the June workshop.

"My constituents voted for this fee because they were promised results," Bergosh said. "I can't keep telling them to wait. These are the same neighborhoods that flooded during Sally. They flooded during the 2014 event. They've been flooding my entire time in office."

Commissioner Lumon May, representing District 3 which includes Brent, noted the disparity between fee revenue and actual need.

"We told voters this fee would make a difference," May said. "We didn't tell them it would take a decade to see that difference."

Flood Risk Unchanged

The National Weather Service's Climate Prediction Center projects an above-average Atlantic hurricane season for 2026. Forecasters expect 14 to 20 named storms, with four to seven becoming major hurricanes.

Escambia County Emergency Management Director Eric Gilmore said flooding remains the primary threat to life and property during tropical weather. Most hurricane deaths in Northwest Florida result from freshwater flooding, not storm surge or wind.

"Our drainage systems are the first line of defense," Gilmore said. "When they're compromised, water has nowhere to go."

The county's most flood-prone areas overlap significantly with its stormwater project backlog. FEMA flood maps show portions of Brownsville, Brent, and Myrtle Grove in moderate-to-high risk zones. Many homes in these neighborhoods predate modern flood insurance requirements. Residents often lack coverage.

Williams, the Brownsville homeowner, said he's spent $4,000 on sandbags and temporary barriers over the past five years. His flood insurance premium jumped 40% after the 2020 storm season.

"I pay my taxes. I pay this new fee," Williams said. "And I'm still out here every storm filling sandbags like I'm protecting myself from the county, not the weather."

What Comes Next

County staff will present a revised stormwater capital plan at the July commission meeting. Gonzalez said the plan will prioritize projects based on flood risk, cost efficiency, and "shovel readiness"—how quickly work can actually begin.

The county is also pursuing federal grant funding through FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program. A $6 million application for Brownsville drainage improvements is pending. Awards are expected in late 2026.

Commissioner May suggested the county consider bond financing to accelerate the backlog, using stormwater fee revenue for debt service. That approach would require voter approval.

"We can keep going project by project for the next 10 years," May said. "Or we can have an honest conversation about what it actually costs to fix this."

No commissioners committed to putting a bond measure on the ballot.

Meanwhile, hurricane season continues through November. The next named storm to threaten the Gulf Coast will find Escambia County's drainage infrastructure largely where it was a year ago. And the year before that.

Williams has already bought this year's sandbags. They're stacked in his garage, waiting.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Quiet Transformation of West Cervantes Street
articles.dek: Between I-110 and A Street, auto shops and vacant lots are giving way to breweries, a climbing gym, and market-rate apartments. Long-time business owners wonder whether they're watching revitalization or replacement.
brief: West Cervantes Street between I-110 and A Street has seen at least seven new businesses open since 2024, with three more developments under construction.
Commercial property values along the corridor have increased 40% since 2022, according to Escambia County Property Appraiser records.
Long-time business owners express mixed feelings about changes that bring foot traffic but also rising rents and shifting customer demographics.
articles.body:
The transmission shop at 1847 West Cervantes still smells like gear oil and hot metal. Eddie Ramos has worked here for 31 years, first as a mechanic, then as owner after buying the place from his boss in 2009. On a Thursday morning in late June, he's watching a crew across the street frame out what will become a 24-unit apartment building.

"When I started here, this was the edge of town nobody cared about," Ramos said. "Now I got people asking if I want to sell every other week."

He does not want to sell.

The stretch of West Cervantes between Interstate 110 and A Street—roughly a mile of four-lane road running parallel to the railroad tracks—spent decades as a corridor of necessity rather than destination. Transmission shops. Used tire dealers. A welding supply company. Vacant lots gone to weeds. The kind of street you drove through on your way somewhere else.

That street is disappearing. In its place, something new is taking shape. Whether that something serves the people who built their lives here is an open question.

The New Arrivals

Iron Rail Brewing opened in a converted warehouse at 1912 West Cervantes in March 2024. The building had housed a janitorial supply company for 40 years before sitting empty for three. Now it pours craft beer to crowds that spill onto a patio built where delivery trucks once backed in.

"We looked at five or six locations around town," said Marcus Webb, one of Iron Rail's three co-owners. "This one had the bones. High ceilings, good parking, room to grow. And the price was right."

That price—$425,000 for a 6,200-square-foot building on half an acre—would be impossible to replicate today. Comparable properties on the corridor now list for $650,000 or more, according to commercial real estate listings.

Iron Rail wasn't first. A climbing gym called Limestone opened in 2022, taking over a former boat storage facility. A coffee roaster set up shop in 2023. A CrossFit gym. A pottery studio. Each new business seemed to validate the next.

"There's momentum now," said Rachel Odom, who opened Perdido Pottery at 1734 West Cervantes last September. "People are actually walking around here. That didn't happen three years ago."

The Numbers

Escambia County Property Appraiser records tell one version of the story. Commercial assessed values on parcels along West Cervantes between I-110 and A Street have risen 40% since 2022. Residential parcels in the surrounding blocks—an area bounded roughly by Cervantes, Gonzalez, W Street, and the railroad—have seen assessed values climb 28% in the same period.

Building permit data from Pensacola's Development Services Department shows 14 new commercial permits and 23 residential permits issued for the corridor since January 2024. The largest: a 24-unit market-rate apartment complex at 1830 West Cervantes, currently under construction with a projected completion date in early 2027.

The apartments will rent for between $1,450 and $1,850 per month, according to filings with the city. Median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in Pensacola stood at $1,175 in May 2026, according to data from Apartment List.

No affordable housing units are planned for the development. The developer, Coastline Properties LLC, did not respond to requests for comment.

The View From Here

Sylvia Tran has run Tran's Alterations from a small storefront at 1756 West Cervantes for 18 years. Her lease is up in October. Her landlord has indicated rent will increase from $1,100 per month to $1,650.

"I don't know if I can make that work," Tran said. "My customers, they're working people. They're not going to pay more for hemming just because my rent goes up."

Tran said she's been looking at spaces in the Brownsville area and near the Fairfield Drive corridor. Both would take her away from the customers who've found her over nearly two decades.

"I keep hearing the word 'revitalization,'" she said. "Revitalize means bring back to life, right? But we were already alive here. Just not the kind of alive they wanted."

Three doors down, Luis Garza has operated West Side Auto Glass since 2011. His landlord—he owns the building—means he's insulated from rent increases. But he's watching his customer base change.

"The brewery people, they don't need windshields replaced," Garza said. "They Uber home. The climbing gym people, same thing. Young professionals, nice cars under warranty. They go to the dealer."

His revenue is down 15% compared to 2023, Garza said. He's considering whether to sell the building and relocate to a less expensive part of town.

"If I sell now, I do okay," he said. "If I wait, maybe I do better. Or maybe the people buying decide they don't need an auto glass shop here anymore."

The City's Position

The City of Pensacola does not have a formal redevelopment plan for the West Cervantes corridor. Unlike the downtown Community Redevelopment Area or the Eastside CRA, the stretch between I-110 and A Street operates without dedicated tax-increment financing or targeted incentive programs.

"What you're seeing on West Cervantes is market-driven development," said Pensacola Planning Director Amanda Hargrove. "The city's role has been primarily permitting and ensuring compliance with existing zoning."

The corridor is zoned C-1, general commercial, which allows for the mix of uses now emerging. No rezoning has been required for any of the recent projects.

Hargrove said the city has received no formal requests for historic preservation review on the corridor, though at least three buildings—including the former Pensacola Ice Company warehouse at 1880 West Cervantes—are more than 50 years old.

"We respond to applications," Hargrove said. "We don't initiate preservation unless there's a specific request or a structure is already on a register."

What Comes Next

Development Services records show three additional projects in the permitting pipeline for West Cervantes: a mixed-use building with ground-floor retail and 12 apartments above, a restaurant with a rooftop bar, and a self-storage facility.

Real estate agents describe the corridor as "emerging" in listings. That word appears 11 times in active commercial listings for the area, according to a search of LoopNet conducted June 28.

At Iron Rail Brewing on a Friday evening, the patio is full. A band sets up near the loading dock doors, still painted with the faded logo of the janitorial supply company. Across the street, Eddie Ramos's transmission shop is dark, closed for the weekend.

"I've got maybe 10 more years of work in me," Ramos said earlier that week. "I'd like to do them here. But I'm not making any bets."

He gestured toward the apartment construction next door, where workers in hard hats moved behind temporary fencing.

"Ask me again when those are full," he said. "Then we'll know what this street is becoming."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola Expands Flight Training Hours, Drawing Noise Complaints From East Hill
articles.dek: The base added evening and weekend slots to address a pilot training backlog. Residents within two miles say they weren't consulted. Base officials point to a 2019 compatibility study that anticipated the increase.
brief: NAS Pensacola extended flight training operations to include evenings until 10 p.m. and Saturday mornings beginning June 15
East Hill residents report 40% increase in noise complaints to the base's community liaison office since the schedule change
Base officials cite a 2019 Joint Land Use Study that projected expanded operations as pilot training demands increased
articles.body:
The T-6B Texan II banked hard over Bayview Park at 8:47 on a Tuesday evening, its turboprop engine drowning out the little league game below. Parents in the bleachers looked up. Some covered their ears. The plane completed its turn and headed back toward the runways at NAS Pensacola, a mile and a half to the southwest.

Scenes like this have become routine in East Hill since June 15, when the naval air station expanded its flight training schedule to include operations until 10 p.m. on weekdays and Saturday mornings from 7 a.m. to noon. The change adds roughly 18 hours of weekly flight time to address what base officials describe as a persistent backlog in the Navy's pilot training pipeline.

"We understand the adjustment affects our neighbors," said Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Torres, public affairs officer for NAS Pensacola. "The expansion was necessary to meet current training requirements and reduce delays that were affecting fleet readiness."

The backlog stems from pandemic-era disruptions that compressed training schedules and a subsequent surge in pilot candidates. According to Naval Air Training Command data, student naval aviators at Pensacola were waiting an average of 11 weeks between training phases in early 2026, up from a historical average of four weeks.

East Hill residents say they received no direct notice before the schedule change took effect.

"I found out when a plane flew over my house at 9:30 at night," said Marcus Webb, who has lived on North Baylen Street for 22 years. "Nobody knocked on my door. Nobody sent a letter. Nothing."

Webb is among 47 residents who have filed formal noise complaints with the base's community liaison office since mid-June, according to records obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request. The office received 33 complaints during the same period last year.

The 2019 study

Base officials point to the Pensacola Joint Land Use Study completed in 2019 as evidence that expanded operations were anticipated. The 280-page document, commissioned jointly by Escambia County and the Navy, included projections showing flight operations could increase by up to 25% by 2030 to meet training demands.

"The JLUS was a public process with multiple community meetings," Torres said. "The potential for expanded hours was discussed extensively."

The study recommended that Escambia County adopt noise overlay zones limiting residential density near the base and suggested the Navy establish a "community notification protocol" for operational changes. The county adopted the zoning recommendations in 2021. The notification protocol was never formalized.

Pensacola City Council member Teniade Broughton, whose District 6 includes portions of East Hill, said the 2019 study doesn't absolve the base of responsibility to communicate directly with affected residents.

"A planning document from seven years ago isn't the same as picking up the phone," Broughton said. "People have a right to know when something's going to change their daily life."

Measuring the impact

The Navy conducts noise monitoring at three fixed stations around NAS Pensacola. Data from the East Hill station, located near the intersection of Cervantes Street and 12th Avenue, shows average evening decibel readings increased from 58 to 67 since the schedule expansion. Prolonged exposure to sounds above 70 decibels can cause hearing damage, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The readings represent averages. Individual overflights register significantly higher. A T-6B at typical training altitude produces approximately 85 decibels at ground level directly beneath its flight path.

Dr. Linda Okafor, an audiologist at Baptist Hospital who lives in East Hill, said the health effects extend beyond hearing.

"Sleep disruption is the immediate concern," Okafor said. "But chronic noise exposure is linked to elevated cortisol, cardiovascular stress, cognitive impacts in children. These aren't trivial concerns."

The base offers a soundproofing assistance program for homes within designated noise zones, but the program has a three-year waitlist and covers only structures built before 1988.

What happens next

Torres said the expanded schedule is considered permanent but subject to review. The base plans to hold a community listening session in August, though no date has been announced.

Some residents aren't waiting. A group calling itself East Hill Quiet Skies has retained Pensacola attorney David Hutchinson to explore legal options. Hutchinson declined to discuss specifics but confirmed he is reviewing whether the schedule change required additional environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act.

"The 2019 JLUS was a planning document, not a NEPA analysis," Hutchinson said. "Those are different animals."

Webb, the North Baylen Street resident, said he supports the military mission but believes the base could have handled the rollout differently.

"My father was Navy. I'm not anti-military," he said. "But you don't just change people's lives and not even tell them it's coming. That's not how neighbors treat each other."

The next scheduled community liaison meeting between NAS Pensacola and neighborhood representatives is July 18. The meeting is open to the public and will be held at the Bayview Community Center at 6 p.m.
